content: The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes that the designations and presentation of material in its publications do not reflect any opinion regarding the legal status of countries, territories, cities, or their authorities, nor do they address the delimitation of boundaries. While the WHO takes reasonable precautions to verify the accuracy of the information provided, the material is distributed without any warranty, either expressed or implied. The responsibility for interpreting and using the material lies with the reader. Deinfibulation for Type III Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) Deinfibulation, a surgical procedure to open the vaginal opening in women with Type III FGM, has been studied for its role in preventing and treating complications. A 2015 study (in preparation) by Okusanya BO, Oduwole OA, Nwachukwu NS, and Meremikwu M assessed its effectiveness. The quality of evidence was rated as very low due to significant limitations, including bias in case selection, small sample sizes, and wide confidence intervals. For example, one study reported 43 fewer complications per 1,000 women (ranging from 83 fewer to 61 more), but the evidence was deemed critical and unreliable. Timing of Deinfibulation: Antepartum vs. Intrapartum The timing of deinfibulation, whether performed during pregnancy (antepartum) or during labor (intrapartum), has been evaluated for its impact on childbirth outcomes in women with Type III FGM. A 2015 study (in preparation) by Ekpereonne E, Udo A, Okusanya BO, Agamse D, and Meremikwu M found very low-quality evidence, with 14 fewer complications per 1,000 women (ranging from 263 fewer to 175 more). The evidence was downgraded due to risks of bias, uncertainty in effect estimates, and wide overlapping confidence intervals. Counseling Prior to Deinfibulation Counseling women with Type III FGM before undergoing deinfibulation has been explored as an intervention. A 2015 study (in preparation) by Bello S, Ogugbue M, Chibuzor MT, Okomo U, and Meremikwu M reported very low-quality evidence. The study found 107 fewer complications per 1,000 women (ranging from 226 fewer to 122 more), but the findings were limited by small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and potential bias in participant selection. Providing Information to Improve Body Image and Care-Seeking Behavior Providing information to women and girls living with FGM to improve body image and encourage care-seeking behavior has been studied. A 2015 study (in preparation) by Okoye I, Arikpo I, Nwadiaro R, and Meremikwu M found very low-quality evidence, with 119 more women per 1,000 (ranging from 52 more to 205 more) showing improved outcomes. However, the evidence was limited by significant statistical heterogeneity, imprecision, and reliance on a single small study. Educating Healthcare Providers on FGM Consequences Educating healthcare providers about the consequences of FGM to improve their attitudes and client satisfaction has been evaluated. A 2015 study (in preparation) by Oringanje C, Okoro A, Nwankwo O, and Meremikwu M reported very low-quality evidence, with 154 more women per 1,000 (ranging from 26 fewer to 460 more) experiencing improved outcomes. The evidence was limited by small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and potential bias in participant selection. Clitoral Reconstruction for Sexual Dysfunction The use of clitoral reconstruction to address sexual dysfunction in women with FGM has been reviewed. A systematic review by Abdulcadir J, Rodriguez MI, and Say L (2015) and a PhD thesis by Thonnon C (2014) found very low-quality evidence. One study reported 400 fewer cases of dysfunction per 1,000 women (ranging from 30 fewer to 630 fewer), but the findings were limited by small sample sizes, high loss to follow-up (71%), and the use of non-validated scales. Additionally, some women experienced worsened clitoral response postoperatively, highlighting the need for further research. General Observations Across all interventions, the quality of evidence was consistently rated as very low due to methodological limitations, including risks of bias, small sample sizes, wide confidence intervals, and significant heterogeneity. These findings underscore the need for more robust, high-quality research to guide the management of health complications associated with FGM.
